name: Gua sha neck / lymphatic drainage

lead: Gua sha is a traditional Chinese medicine practice in which a smooth tool such as a ceramic spoon, coin or jade stone is drawn across oiled skin. A lighter face and neck version spread on social media in 2021 and 2022, where it was promoted for lymphatic drainage, less puffiness, a sharper jaw and neck line, and skin rejuvenation.

Proponents say light strokes move fluid toward lymph nodes and boost circulation, and users report short-lived puffiness changes. Wikipedia reports the practice lacks high-quality evidence of clinical benefit, and no studies of neck or jaw appearance outcomes were found.

paras: People apply oil, then stroke the stone along the neck and jaw toward the ears and collarbone, usually in a short daily or near-daily routine, often in the morning for debloating. The facial version is gentler than traditional gua sha, which continues until red marks appear.

Traditional gua sha nearly always causes minor skin trauma such as redness or bruising; less common effects include burns, and rare serious harms have been reported. Infection is a concern with unsterilized tools or broken skin.

social.title: What's really going on in lymphatic drainage beauty videos?

chain: Stone scraped along neck and jaw
angle.text: Popularized on social media in 2021 and 2022, gua sha along the jaw and neck is used for debloating, a sharper jawline and skin glow, with the stroking said to move fluid toward the lymph nodes. The technique comes from traditional Chinese medicine; clinical studies of these appearance aims have not been found.

lead: Gua sha is a traditional Chinese medicine practice in which a smooth tool, such as a ceramic spoon, coin or jade stone, is drawn across oiled skin.[1] A lighter facial version applied along the jaw, cheeks and neck became popular on social media in 2021 and 2022, where it was promoted for lymphatic drainage and skin rejuvenation.[1]

People use it to reduce morning puffiness and to make the jaw and neck line look more defined. The reasoning on looksmaxxing forums is that fluid retention in the face blurs bone structure and the jawline, so moving that fluid out makes underlying structure show more clearly.[2][3] Gua sha is usually combined with face massage, cardio and sleep or sinus care in these routines.[2]

Manual lymphatic drainage, the gentle massage technique the facial routines borrow from, has been studied mainly in lymphoedema patients.[4][5] Wikipedia describes gua sha itself as lacking high-quality evidence of clinical benefit, and no trial has measured jaw or neck contour outcomes from facial gua sha.[1]
infobox: Traditional Chinese medicine; formal use from the Ming Dynasty (1368 to 1644)
Ceramic, jade or other smooth stones

paras: Traditional gua sha uses firm, one-direction strokes on oiled skin until small red or purple marks called sha appear.[1] Similar scraping may date to the Paleolithic, and its formal use in traditional Chinese medicine emerged during the Ming Dynasty; it is also linked to the Shanghan Lun, circa 220 CE.[1]

In 2021 and 2022 facial gua sha spread on TikTok, promoted by beauty influencers for lymphatic drainage and skin rejuvenation; the New York Times covered the trend in September 2022.[1] BBC coverage of lymphatic drainage beauty videos has examined what the massages do to the body, noting fans' claims that they depuff and define.[6]

A looksmax.org guide to lymphatic drainage describes a routine of face massages several times a day, optional gua sha, icing and jump rope cardio, and says consistency matters most.[2] Another thread argues that lymphatic congestion from poor sleep, sinus congestion, inflammation or posture can blur jawline definition even in people with strong bone structure.[3]

Wikipedia reports that traditional gua sha nearly always causes minor skin trauma such as redness, bruising or dermatitis; less common effects include burns, and rare serious harms include brain bleeding and injuries needing skin grafts.[1] Infection is a concern with unsterilized tools or open wounds.[1] Facial versions use lighter pressure than the traditional method.

No studies found of facial or neck gua sha for jaw contour, puffiness or lymphatic drainage. Related research on manual lymphatic drainage massage is mostly in patients with lymphoedema: a systematic review examined its effectiveness for people at risk of or living with lymphoedema, and overview articles summarise its use in that condition.[4][5]
